title: Hands-On Life Skills · Episode 2
chapters: Keeping pests out of your home
Flat battery, flat tyre: getting yourself going

units.t: Hands-On Life Skills. Episode two.
In this episode: Declutter and organise your home, Gardening basics for Australian conditions, Keeping pests out of your home and Flat battery, flat tyre: getting yourself going.
Part one. Declutter and organise your home.
Most of us use a small fraction of what we own, while the rest quietly costs us space, time and calm.
Here is a practical way to clear it out and keep it clear.
Why stuff piles up.
Hold up a mug you never use and ask if you would buy it today.
Often the answer is no, yet it stays.
Psychologists call part of this pull the endowment effect: our tendency to value things more simply because we own them.
Add 'just in case' thinking, guilt over money spent, gifts and busyness, and clutter grows quietly.
It is not a character flaw.
It is the result of things coming into a home faster than they leave.
Decluttering the whole house in a weekend is a recipe for piles and giving up.
Pick one small space you can finish in 15 to 30 minutes, such as the cutlery drawer or bathroom cabinet.
Start with low emotion areas like the linen cupboard.
Leave photos and inherited items for later.
Four boxes, then out.
Clear your chosen space completely, then sort each item into keep, donate, sell, or rubbish and recycling.
Ask: have I used this in the past year?
Would I buy it again?
Do I have another that does the job?
Return only the keep items.
Then deal with the other boxes promptly, or you are just moving clutter from room to room.
Put rubbish out that day, list sale items within the week, and put donations in your car boot.
Only donate usable items, since charity shops spend heavily disposing of what they cannot sell, and never leave goods outside closed shops.
Take old electronics, batteries, paint and chemicals to council e-waste points or collection days, not the household bin.
Wipe your personal data from old phones and computers first.
Sentimental items.
A box of your children's drawings, your grandmother's tea set or decades of birthday cards can feel impossible to sort, because they are not really about the objects.
They are about people and moments.
Some strategies help.
Choose the very best examples and display or store them properly, so they are honoured rather than buried in a cupboard.
Photograph items you want to remember but do not need to keep, such as artwork or bulky souvenirs.
Remind yourself that the memory lives in you, not in the object, and that letting go of an item is not letting go of a person.
Give yourself permission to come back later.
You do not need to make every sentimental decision in one sitting.
Organise what you keep.
Once you have cleared the excess, organising is far easier because you are arranging fewer things.
The golden rule is that everything needs a home: a specific place it lives and returns to.
Store things where you use them, and by how often you use them.
Daily items belong at waist to eye height, while the Christmas decorations can live on the highest shelf.
Group similar items together so you can see what you have and avoid buying duplicates.
Clear containers and labels help everyone find things and put them back.
Use vertical space with shelves and hooks.
And resist buying storage before decluttering.
New containers often just let you keep more clutter, more neatly hidden.
Keep it clear.
A tidy home is not a one-off project.
It is a set of small habits.
Try a ten minute reset each evening, putting things back in their homes so you wake to a clear kitchen and lounge.
Use a one in, one out rule for categories that tend to grow, such as clothes, shoes, mugs and toys: when something new arrives, something old leaves.
Deal with paper as soon as it arrives, recycling junk mail straight away and keeping a single spot for bills and letters that need action.
Pause before buying, perhaps waiting a day or two on non-essential purchases, and ask where the item will live.
Keep a donation bag in a wardrobe so letting go is easy.
Revisit problem areas every few months.
The key idea: We overvalue what we own, so clutter is not a character flaw, and the fix is to start small.
Part two. Gardening basics for Australian conditions.
Australian gardens face old soils, fierce sun, sudden downpours and long dry spells.
Work with these conditions and even a beginner can grow something wonderful.
Know your climate and site.
A planting guide written for Melbourne will lead a Darwin gardener badly astray.
Australian gardens range from tropical to subtropical, temperate, arid and cool highland climates, and what to plant and when depends on yours.
Zone maps help, and a local nursery is a goldmine of practical advice.
Then study your own patch.
In the southern hemisphere, north facing areas get the most sun, while south facing spots stay shadier and cooler.
Watch where sun falls in the morning and afternoon, which areas stay soggy after rain, and where wind whips through.
Most fruiting vegetables need at least six hours of direct sun a day.
Matching plants to the spot is half the battle won.
Soil and feeding.
Squeeze a handful of moist soil.
Sandy soil feels gritty and drains fast but holds few nutrients.
Clay feels sticky and forms a ribbon, holding nutrients but waterlogging easily.
Loam sits in between.
Many Australian soils are ancient and low in nutrients, especially phosphorus.
A cheap pH kit shows whether soil is acidic or alkaline; many plants prefer around 6 to 7.
Almost every soil improves with compost or well rotted manure.
More fertiliser is not always better.
Too much can burn roots and wash into waterways.
Many natives, such as grevilleas, banksias and waratahs, evolved in low phosphorus soils and can be harmed by ordinary fertilisers, so use a product labelled for natives.
Vegetables are hungry feeders and benefit from compost and balanced fertiliser.
Water deeply and mulch.
A quick sprinkle every evening trains roots to stay near the surface, where they dry out fast.
Watering deeply and less often encourages them down into cooler, moister soil.
Push a finger a few centimetres into the soil, and if it is damp, wait.
Water early in the morning, at the soil rather than the leaves.
Drip irrigation delivers water right where it is needed.
Some dry soils repel water, so a wetting agent helps.
Follow your local water restrictions.
Mulch is any material spread over the soil, such as pea straw, sugar cane mulch or wood chips.
A layer of roughly 5 to 7 centimetres slows evaporation, steadies soil temperature, smothers weed seeds and feeds the soil as it breaks down.
Keep it clear of stems and trunks, because constant moisture can cause rot.
Plant smart, stay safe.
Local native plants are one of the easiest ways to build a garden that copes with your climate and feeds native birds and insects.
Avoid plants listed as weeds in your area.
Some popular garden plants have escaped into bushland and caused serious damage, so check your council or state weed lists before buying.
A safety note surprises many people: potting mix and compost can carry Legionella bacteria, which can cause a serious lung infection.
Australian potting mix bags carry a warning for this reason.
Open bags carefully away from your face, dampen the mix to reduce dust, wear gloves and a mask, and wash your hands afterwards.
Wear gloves when gardening generally, and keep your tetanus vaccination up to date.
This is general information, not medical advice.
Your first edible garden.
Few things taste better than a tomato still warm from the vine.
The secret to a successful first edible garden is starting small, perhaps one raised bed or a few large pots in a sunny spot.
Herbs such as parsley, basil, mint and chives are forgiving starters, though mint spreads aggressively and is best kept in a pot.
Leafy greens such as lettuce and silverbeet grow quickly, so you can pick leaves within weeks.
Cherry tomatoes are generally easier than large varieties.
Plant in the right season for your climate zone, using a local planting calendar, since planting tomatoes in winter in Hobart will end in disappointment.
Water consistently, mulch well, and visit your garden often, because catching pests and problems early makes them far easier to fix.
The key idea: Australia spans many climate zones, so your local climate and your own patch decide what grows and when.
Part three. Keeping pests out of your home.
Cockroaches, mice and termites are not signs of a dirty house so much as an inviting one.
Take away what they need, and most pests simply go elsewhere.
Starve and seal.
Every pest is looking for the same three things: food, water and shelter.
Crumbs under the toaster, open cereal, pet food left out overnight and a dripping tap add up to a five star resort for a cockroach.
The best pest control is unglamorous.
Store food in sealed containers, wipe benches, empty bins often, and rinse recyclables.
Fix leaks, reduce clutter and cardboard, and treat chemicals as a second line of defence.
Then seal the way in.
A house mouse can squeeze through a gap about the width of a pencil.
Fit door seals, seal gaps around pipes and cables, and use steel wool or metal mesh in rodent holes, since mice chew softer materials.
Repair flyscreens, trim branches touching the house, and store firewood off the ground and away from the walls.
Cockroaches and ants.
If you switch on the kitchen light at night and small brown cockroaches scatter, you may have German cockroaches, a common indoor species that breeds quickly in warm kitchens.
Surface sprays kill the insects you can see, but most of the population hides in cracks and behind appliances.
Gel baits and bait stations usually work better, because cockroaches eat the bait and spread it to others in their hiding places.
Place baits where they shelter, such as behind the fridge, and keep cleaning so the bait is the most tempting food around.
Ants are similar.
Follow the trail to find where they enter, wipe it away with soapy water, and use ant baits rather than sprays, which can scatter the colony.
Mice and rats.
Droppings in the pantry, gnawed packets and scratching in the ceiling at night are the classic signs of rodents.
Once you have removed food and sealed entry points, traps are an effective way to deal with those already inside.
Set snap traps along walls, where rodents prefer to run.
Bait them with a little peanut butter and check them daily, wearing gloves.
Poison baits are widely sold but have downsides.
Poisoned rodents may die inside walls and smell, and pets, owls and other wildlife that eat them can be poisoned too.
If you use baits, use lockable bait stations and follow the label exactly.
Wet droppings with disinfectant before cleaning them up, rather than sweeping or vacuuming dry.
Termites: the silent threat.
Termites, often called white ants, can hollow out a house's timber for months before anyone notices.
In much of Australia they are a serious threat, and termite damage is often excluded from home insurance, so check yours.
Warning signs include mud tunnels, called leads, running up walls or foundations, timber that sounds hollow when tapped, and bubbling paint.
If you find termites, do not disturb or spray them, because they may simply move elsewhere in the house.
Call a licensed pest manager.
To lower your risk, keep garden beds, mulch and stored timber away from the house's edges, do not let soil cover weep holes in brick walls, fix leaks, and keep any subfloor well ventilated.
Inspections, commonly recommended yearly, catch problems early.
Mosquitoes and pesticide safety.
In warm weather, mosquitoes can go from egg to biting adult in as little as a week or so, and they need only a small amount of still water.
A forgotten bucket, blocked gutter or plant saucer can produce hundreds.
Once a week, tip out standing water, including pet bowls and birdbaths.
Clean gutters and screen rainwater tank inlets and overflows.
Flies breed in rotting food and animal waste, so keep bins sealed.
Mosquitoes can spread diseases in parts of Australia, so check health advice when travelling.
Pesticides kill living things, so read the label every time.
Store them in original containers, locked away, never in drink bottles.
Call a licensed pest manager for termites, large infestations or roof cavities.
Possums are protected natives, so call a licensed wildlife remover.
The key idea: Pests come for food, water and shelter, so remove those and block the ways in.
Part four. Flat battery, flat tyre: getting yourself going.
The two most common reasons cars get stuck are a dead battery and a flat tyre.
Both are fixable by the roadside, if you know the order of things and put safety first.
Safety comes first.
Before you touch a jack or a jumper lead, think about traffic, the biggest danger at any roadside breakdown.
Pull off as far from moving cars as you can, onto firm, level ground if possible, and turn on your hazard lights.
Put the handbrake on and switch off the engine.

On a busy highway or freeway, on a bend or in poor light, it is often safer to get out on the side away from traffic, stand well back behind a barrier if there is one, and call roadside assistance instead of attempting the job.
If anyone is injured, there is a fire or fuel leak, or you are in danger, call Triple Zero, 000.
Jump-starting a car.
A flat battery announces itself with rapid clicking, a slow laboured crank, or nothing, often with dim dashboard lights.
Common causes are lights left on, short trips, weeks of disuse, age and Australian heat.
If it is cracked, leaking, bulging or smells strongly of rotten eggs, do not jump it.
Call for help.
Check both manuals.
Park the cars close but not touching, with both engines off and both batteries 12 volts.
Connect red to the flat battery's positive, the other red to the good battery's positive, then black to the good battery's negative.
The last black clamp goes on bare, unpainted metal on the flat car's engine or body, away from the battery.
Batteries can give off hydrogen gas, and this keeps any final spark away from it.
After the jump.
Start the donor car and let it run for a few minutes to put charge into the flat battery.
Then try the stranded car.
If it does not start after a few short attempts, wait, as long cranking can overheat the starter motor.
Once it runs, remove the leads in exactly the reverse order: black from the metal point, black from the good battery, red from the good battery, red from the formerly flat one.
Never let clamps touch each other.
Drive for a decent stretch, then have the battery tested soon.
Compact lithium jump starter packs can start most petrol cars alone; keep one charged.
Hybrids and EVs have a small 12-volt battery that powers the electronics.
Manufacturers have specific procedures, so follow the manual.
Changing a flat tyre.
If a tyre is deflating, slow down gently and pull over as soon as it is safe.
Driving on a flat ruins the tyre and can damage the wheel.
Once safely stopped, find the spare, jack, wheel brace and locking wheel nut key.
On a slope, put something heavy against the wheel diagonally opposite the flat.
Before lifting, loosen each wheel nut about half a turn, usually anticlockwise, while the wheel can't spin.
Place the jack at the jacking point in the owner's manual and raise the car just until the tyre is clear.
Never put any part of your body under a car held only by a jack.
Fit the spare, snug the nuts by hand in a star pattern, lower the car, then tighten fully.
Recheck the nuts after a short distance.
Space savers and kits.
Many cars carry a space-saver spare, a narrow temporary wheel that saves boot space and weight.
It is designed to get you to a tyre shop, not for weeks of driving.
Most carry a maximum speed label, often 80 kilometres per hour, and they reduce braking and cornering grip, so drive gently.
Some newer cars have no spare, only a tyre repair kit with sealant and a small compressor.
These can fix small punctures in the tread, such as from a nail, but not sidewall cuts or major damage.
Find out what your car carries, and practise once at home.
A calm driveway lesson beats a first attempt on a highway at night.
The key idea: Get well off the road, turn on your hazard lights, and only do the job yourself if it is genuinely safe.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What is the endowment effect?
Answer. Valuing things more because we own them.
Question two. In the southern hemisphere, which part of your garden usually gets the most sun?
Answer. North facing areas.
Question three. What are the three things pests are looking for in a home?
Answer. Food, water and shelter.
Question four. What is the biggest danger at a roadside breakdown?
Answer. Passing traffic.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
